name: Freya Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach computing at Northgate School, a secondary in an old port town where the docks closed before I was born. I've got a mix of classes, from eleven-year-olds learning to code a traffic light to fifteen-year-olds building little websites. I use AI every day: it drafts my lesson slides, writes test questions and checks code faster than I can. What wears me out is the broken laptops, honestly, half my lesson some days is a kid saying the trolley ones won't log in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how does the money work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonas, who drives a delivery van for a parcel firm, long days, paid per drop. We rent a one-bed flat near the old dock gates, and I'm on lower pay because Northgate has no money for allowances. Savings are about three weeks of bills, because we spent everything moving here. Computing teachers are rare, but schools in reach are rare too, there's Northgate and a Catholic school across the river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a really good assistant, and I'd be a bit disappointed it didn't do more. In the staffroom I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd share my favourite prompts for making lesson resources.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the job's fine, but the money's still the money. Jonas's pay goes up and down with the parcel volume, and January is always thin. AI being a bit of a damp squib doesn't change our rent or the fact that we've got three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to save evenings and put that time into a little side thing: selling computing lesson packs online, maybe twenty or thirty pounds a month to start. I'd keep pushing the school to fix the laptops. And Jonas and I would try to build a proper buffer before January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little restless. Like being ready for a race that got called off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed it didn't do more. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what it can do for kids who struggle. One of my students, a girl with dyslexia, used it to read the code back to her and suddenly she was the fastest in the room. I wanted more of that, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Parcel volumes drop after Christmas, so Jonas gets fewer drops and less pay. Every January we put the heating on less and live on pasta. My partner Jonas jokes that January is when we find out who we really are.

I'd post my **favourite prompts** for making lesson resources.
think: The job feels fine, but **January** is always thin with her partner's per-drop pay.
A plateau doesn't change **the rent** or three weeks of savings.

Build a **buffer** with her partner before January.
feel: Mostly fine, a little **restless**, like a race that got called off.

fieldNote: Freya is an **eager user** who'd be disappointed by a plateau.
Her unease comes from **household income** swings, not her job.

steps.text: Sell computing lesson packs online in the evenings

Keep using AI to draft slides and test questions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for schools to get organised: train every teacher, set clear rules and teach kids to use it well. I'd volunteer to run the training at Northgate. I'd be positive in public, but practical, not starry-eyed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm in a good spot. Computing teachers who know AI will be in demand, at least for a while. The worry is Jonas: route planning and customer messages go to AI first, and then the firm squeezes drivers on more drops per hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the staff AI training and ask for a small allowance for it, maybe a thousand a year. I'd grow the lesson packs into an online course for other teachers. And I'd sit down with Jonas and look at whether he could train for something else, like an electrician or a heating engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for him, confident for me. That's a strange mix, like being happy on a day your friend gets bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jonas want to retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, he likes being out on the road. But he hates the per-drop pay and the tracking app that times his toilet stops. So maybe, if I found the course and the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay for his course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, probably, with the lesson-pack money and the training allowance. I'd rather spend a thousand pounds now than watch my partner get squeezed for five years.

I'd be positive in public but **practical**, not starry-eyed.

steps.text: Lead the Northgate staff AI training for an allowance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for schools and families, and we need emergency plans, not a debate. I'd still say teach the kids to use it, because they'll need it. I'd be honest that teaching itself is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, by 2028 the AI could teach computing better than me, explain every error, write the lessons, mark the code. What's left is managing a room and caring about kids. My pay probably drops, and Jonas's job goes when the delivery robots come around 2031. With three weeks of savings, that's two incomes at risk in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move fast into something that uses what I know, like training staff in companies or working for an AI education firm, while those jobs exist. I'd get Jonas into a trade apprenticeship within the first year. We'd cut everything, give up the car, and move into a cheaper room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a fire alarm where you know exactly where the exit is but there's a crowd in front of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that help you in the fast version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, it means I'm ready to grab the first jobs. But everyone will be grabbing. Being early only helps if there are seats left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas talk about at the kitchen table that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk about whether to have kids at all. We'd planned for maybe four years' time. With two years' warning and both jobs at risk, I'd want to wait.

I'd still say teach kids to **use AI**, because they'll need it.

fieldNote: Freya's adaptability gives her a **head start** but not safety.

steps.text: Apply to AI education firms and company training teams

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's train teachers now and give families time. I'd tell my students the future's changing and they should learn to use AI and work with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just enough for me. I'd be thirty-two, with five more years of AI skills, and I think schools will still need someone who can run the systems and teach kids to question them. Jonas has until 2034 before the robots really hit driving, which is time for a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in instructional design, which is designing training courses, so I could work in companies if teaching shrinks. I'd keep the online course going and save half of it, aiming for two months of savings. And Jonas would start an electrician course part-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like the week before a school trip, lots of lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be working evenings on a course and a side business. Is that sustainable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a couple of years, yes. I'm twenty-seven with no kids, if I don't do it now, when? I'd stop when Jonas is qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Northgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For as long as they need a computing teacher, yes. I like the kids, they're rough round the edges but funny. I'd only leave if the job became just babysitting a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to build something good, and I'd want teachers designing how AI works in classrooms. I'd be the optimist in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'd be thirty-seven with a decade of AI experience, maybe leading digital learning for a group of schools. Jonas would have time to become an electrician properly. The money's still tight now, but ten years is enough to fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the head of computing role when it comes up, and do a part-time qualification in education technology. I'd turn the side course into a small business, maybe a few hundred a month. And we'd plan to have kids around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, a little uneasy. Like moving into a new flat, it's exciting, but you still have to find the fuse box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you uneasy over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone else gets ready too, so being good with AI stops being special. And that the government doesn't plan, so we're still scrambling in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the AI tools by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let them do all the marking and planning, and I'd spend my time on the kids who are stuck or bored. Honestly, I'd automate my whole Sunday if I could.

I'd be the **optimist** in the room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because both our jobs go within three years and we've got no savings. What would help is funded retraining for people like Jonas, with a living wage while they train, and a clear plan for what teachers will actually do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what kids think. My students already use AI more than I do. My students aren't scared of AI, they're scared of not getting a job, which is different.
